unit.title: Invest like the winners
unit.description: Indices, ETFs, diversification and investing every month: the simple portfolio that works long term

texts: The fund that made 8 %
Marta
My fund made 8 % this year! That's brilliant, right?
That year, the index for its market rose 14 %.
What do you tell Marta?
Congratulations: 8 % is great
Sounds good… but copying the index would have given her 14 %.
It came in 6 points behind its index
Exactly. That's what an index is for: it's the **yardstick**.
It depends how much money she put in
The amount doesn't change the percentage: 8 % versus 14 %.
So how do I buy that index?
You can't buy it as such: you buy a **fund or ETF** that tracks it.
What's an index for?
An **index** sums up in one figure how a group of securities is doing. It's used for three things.
Thermometer
Yardstick
Basis for products
«The Spanish stock market is up 1 % today»
That's the IBEX 35: it tells you how the market is doing.
A fund compares its performance with the IBEX 35
The index is the benchmark for knowing whether the fund did well.
An ETF that copies the S&P 500
ETFs and index funds track it at low cost.
Finding out how the banking sector is doing today
There are country and sector indices: more specific thermometers.
Checking whether your portfolio did well
Compare it with an index that resembles what you hold.
An index fund to pay into every month
The index fund copies the index: that's how you «buy» it.
Sort the six uses.
An index is a **thermometer**, a **yardstick** and a **basis for products**. Each one has its own rules: which companies get in, how much each one weighs and how often it's reviewed.
Hint: does it inform, help you compare, or get bought as a fund?
One figure with lots of different jobs.
Tap each case: what's the index used for?

steps.title: Points, not euros
steps.body: An index is measured in points, not euros. What matters is the **change**: if it goes from 14,000 to 14,700 points, it's up 5 %.
steps.key: An index is a reference basket, not something you buy as such.
steps.tip: Buying the whole index is betting on an entire economy, not on one company.

texts: ETF or traditional fund?
An **ETF** is a fund, almost always tracking an index, that **trades on the stock exchange** like a share. Is it an ETF thing or a traditional fund thing?
ETF
Traditional fund
You buy it at 11:37 at the price on your screen
An ETF trades all session long: its price changes from moment to moment.
You swap it for another without paying tax
Tax-free transfers are the fund's big advantage in Spain.
You pay the broker's commission and the spread
It's bought on the stock exchange, with the usual trading costs.
Its price is calculated once a day
A fund's net asset value is set once every day.
Every sale at a profit is taxed, even if you reinvest
In Spain, ETFs don't get the fund transfer rules.
You buy it through the management company, a bank or a platform
A traditional fund isn't listed: you subscribe to it directly.
Sort all six features.
An ETF is bought and sold **on the stock exchange, like a share**, and the big ones cost from **0.03 % to 0.30 %** a year. In Spain, the traditional fund has the advantage of **tax-free transfers**.
Hint: is it traded on the stock exchange or not?
Sort each feature
«Like a share»
Nora
Someone told me an ETF is «like a share».
So is it just as risky as buying a single company?
What do you tell her?
Yes, just as risky
You buy it like a share, but inside there are hundreds or thousands of companies.
You buy it like a share, but inside there's a basket of lots of companies
That's it! An MSCI World one holds more than a thousand companies from developed countries.
It has no risk at all
It has the index's risk: if the market falls 30 %, so does the ETF.
An index ETF is like buying the whole supermarket instead of a single product.

steps.title: UCITS ETFs
steps.body: A retail investor in the EU buys European **UCITS** ETFs, which come with a **KID**. Many US ETFs can't be sold to European retail investors because they don't have a KID.
steps.key: An ETF is a fund, almost always an index one, that you buy and sell on the stock exchange like a share.
steps.tip: Before buying an ETF, look for «UCITS» in its name and read its KID.

u29l1.title: Diversifying: the only free thing in finance

texts: All your eggs in one basket
Bruno
I've put my €3,000 into a single company. It's going to be the next big tech giant!
I know it well: I've read everything there is about it.
What do you tell him?
Perfect: if you know it, there's no risk
Knowing it doesn't protect it from fraud, a failed product or bankruptcy.
Spread it out: across lots of companies, one bankruptcy barely shows
That's it! If a company is 0.1 % of your money, its disaster hardly shows.
Buy one more, then you've got two
Better than one, but two companies is still very few.
A single company can fall **90 %**. To recover, you'd need **+900 %**.
Phew. And if I spread it out, is there no risk at all?
There are two kinds of risk. Let's separate them.
One company or all of them?
**Specific** risk hits one particular company. **Market** risk hits them all at once. Which is which?
Specific: one company
Market: all of them
Accounting fraud at a company
It only happens to one: in an index of thousands of companies, it barely shows.
A global recession
It hits almost every company at once: more shares don't dilute it.
A company's flagship product flops
A problem for that company, not for the whole economy.
A pandemic that shuts down the economy
It affects the whole market: spreading across more shares doesn't avoid it.
A long strike at a company's factory
It only slows that company down: its competitors keep selling.
The central bank suddenly raises interest rates
It changes the price of money for every company at once.
Sort the six scares.
Diversifying **removes specific risk**: one bankruptcy weighs little among thousands of companies. **Market risk** doesn't go away with more shares; it's only softened by mixing in bonds or cash.
Ask yourself: does it happen to one company or to the whole economy?
Nicely sorted! Now for the only free lunch.
Sort each scare

steps.title: The free lunch
steps.body:
A single share moves 30-35 % a year; 20-30 shares from different sectors, around 20 %; a global index, 15 %.

Harry Markowitz, Nobel Prize in Economics, called this **the only free lunch**: less risk without giving up expected return.
steps.key: With lots of companies, the disasters of some are offset by the successes of others.
steps.tip: Don't put all your eggs in one basket, or all your baskets on the same lorry.

texts: The price drops… and comes back
Irene
I put €100 into a fund every month, no matter what.
Over five months, the price goes €10, €8, €5, €8 and back to €10.
It's back where it was. I guess I'm where I started.
How is Irene doing?
Same as before: the price ended where it started
No: when it was cheap, her €100 bought more units.
Up: she bought more units when it was cheap
Exactly! She put in €500 and now has €650: **30 %** more.
Down: she bought in the middle of a fall
The opposite: during the fall, the same money got her more units.
Investing **the same amount every month** is called DCA (dollar-cost averaging). Falls work in your favour.
All at once or bit by bit?
You've got **€12,000** for the S&P 500, with real data. All in the first month or spread over 12? See how much you'd have 10 years later.
Looking at every possible starting month, which wins more often over 10 years?
Spreading it out, almost always
All at once, about three times out of four
Half and half
All at once wins in **74 %** of starting months. Vanguard, using the MSCI World from 1976 to 2022, saw it win 68 % of the time after one year.
Find a starting month where spreading it out came out ahead.
**All at once usually wins**, because the market goes up more often than it goes down. **Spreading it out** wins just before a fall and reduces regret, but nobody knows when the fall is coming.
Here spreading it out won! Look what came right after: a fall.
All at once wins by a mile: the market rose from the start.
Move the starting month. Try just before a crisis

steps.title: With a large sum
steps.body:
A sensible middle ground: spread it over **6–12 months** with automatic contributions.

What doesn't work is waiting «for it to drop»: nobody knows where the bottom is.
steps.key: All at once wins more often; bit by bit reduces regret. What matters is starting and not stopping.
steps.tip: Investing every month is like climbing stairs: what matters is not stopping.

u10l3.title: Fees: the TER and hidden costs

texts: The cost you can't see
The same **€10,000** and the same market: 7 % a year before costs. One fund charges **0.2 %** a year; the other, whatever you choose.
Over 30 years, one fund charges 0.2 % and another 1.5 %. How much does the difference take?
Not much: about 1 % of the result
Almost a third of the result
More than half
The cost is charged **every year** and compounds: the cheap one ends at €71,968 and the expensive one at €49,840. That's **€22,128**, or 31 %.
Set the expensive fund to 1.5 % and see what happens over 30 years.
The **TER** (ongoing charges) never arrives as a bill: it's taken little by little out of the fund's value. Over 30 years, 1.5 % a year takes **almost a third** of your money.
Almost a third of your money, gone on fees!
Keep going: with more years, the gap shoots up.
Raise the expensive fund's fee and the years
The star team
Ana
Bank adviser
Ana, I recommend our equity fund. It's run by a star team.
And how much does it charge?
2 % a year. You're paying for quality.
A similar index fund charges 0.2 %.
What should Ana think?
If it's a star team, it's worth it
It would have to beat the index by 1.8 points a year, year after year. Hardly anyone manages that.
The expensive one has to earn 1.8 points more every year just to break even
That's it! The cost is guaranteed; beating the index isn't.
She should try it for a year and compare
One year tells you little: it could be luck. The cost, on the other hand, is always paid.

steps.title: Hidden costs
steps.body:
An index fund might charge 0.1-0.3 % a year; many active funds in Spain, 1.5 % or more. You'll see it in the **KID**, as ongoing charges.

On top of the TER: the broker's commission per trade, *spread*, custody fees, currency exchange and, for some funds, entry or exit fees. Add them all up.
steps.key: Every 1 % a year in costs eats a huge chunk of the result, because of compound interest.
steps.tip: 1.5 % a year sounds like nothing. Over 30 years, it's almost a third of your money.

texts: How long do you have to wait?
Real data: the S&P 500 month by month over 40 years. Imagine you invested in **any** month and waited a few years. How many times would you have lost money?
If you invested in any given month and sold **a year later**, how often did you lose money?
Almost never
Roughly 1 in 5 times
Half the time
Over these 40 years, **20.8 %** of one-year periods ended in a loss, and the worst one lost 45 %.
Find how many years you had to wait for there to be not a single case with a loss.

In this data, waiting **14 years or more** never lost money. But the past doesn't guarantee the future: anyone who bought in 1929, or in Japan in 1989, waited much longer. Your time horizon decides how much risk you can take.
In the short term the stock market is a rollercoaster: almost anything can happen.
Look at the worst case: there are still long periods in the red (the ones that started in 2000).
Keep making the wait longer

steps.title: Put a date on every euro
steps.body:
• **Cushion:** always available interest-paying account, money market fund.
• **Trip or car (1-3 years)** deposits, Treasury bills.
• **Deposit on a flat (3-7 years)** a cautious mix, more bonds.
• **Retirement (15 years or more)** mostly diversified shares.
steps.key: Money you'll need soon doesn't go into the stock market: it could be falling just when you need it.

u7l1-1.prompt: What is a stock market index?
options: A company listed on the stock market
A figure that sums up how a group of securities is doing
u7l1-1.explanation: It's a reference basket with rules about what gets in and how much it weighs.

u7l1-3.prompt: An index goes from 14,000 to 14,700 points. How much has it risen?

u7l1-4.prompt: Quick: an index goes from 5,000 to 4,600 points. How much has it fallen, in %? (enter it as a positive number)

u7l1-6.prompt: If the IBEX 35 is at 14,000 points, buying it costs €14,000.
u7l1-6.explanation: Points aren't euros: they measure the change from a base.

u7l1-7.prompt: What do an index's rules set? Select all that apply.
options: Whatever a TV pundit thinks that day
u7l1-7.explanation: The rules are public and objective: that's why the index works as a benchmark.

u7l1-10.prompt: You can't buy an index directly: you buy a fund or an ____ that tracks it.
u7l1-10.explanation: ETFs and index funds copy the index at low cost.

u10l2-1.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
u10l2-1.explanation: These are the four words you'll see when you look up any ETF.
right: Basket of companies the ETF copies
Fund that trades on the stock exchange

u10l2-3.prompt: This chart is an index that several ETFs copy: an ETF tracking it will do the same, minus its costs. What did it do over the next 10 sessions?
u10l2-3.explanation: An index ETF doesn't remove the market's ups and downs: you get exactly what the index does, for better and for worse.

u10l2-4.prompt: What annual cost do the big index ETFs usually have?
u10l2-4.explanation: Copying an index is cheap: you don't need a team picking companies.

u10l2-6.prompt: Why can't a European retail investor buy many US ETFs?
options: Because investing in dollars is banned
Because they don't have a KID
u10l2-6.explanation: Without a KID, they can't be marketed to retail investors in the EU.

u10l2-7.prompt: You buy 15 units of an ETF at €98.40 and the broker charges a €2 commission. How much do you pay in total?

u10l2-10.prompt: The ETFs a retail investor can buy in the EU usually carry the ____ label.
u10l2-10.explanation: It's the European framework that sets rules on diversification, custody and disclosure.

u29l1-1.prompt: Which risk do you eliminate by spreading your money across hundreds of shares?
u29l1-1.explanation: A bankruptcy stops being a drama if it's 0.1 % of your money. But if the whole market falls, they all fall: that risk is only softened with bonds or cash.

u29l1-2.prompt: You split €10,000 equally across 20 shares. One goes bankrupt and loses all its value; the rest stay the same. How many euros do you lose?
u29l1-2.explanation: 10,000 ÷ 20 = €500 per share. With a single share, that bankruptcy would have wiped out the whole €10,000.

u29l1-4.prompt: Practice exercise (not a recommendation): split €10,000 across these shares. Rules: at least 6 companies, none above 20 % and no sector above 30 %.
u29l1-4.explanation: Spreading across companies and sectors reduces specific risk. Even so, 8 shares is still very few: an index has hundreds or thousands.

u29l1-6.prompt: What is NOT diversifying? Select all that apply.
options: A global share fund and a bond fund
Having almost everything in shares of the company you work for
Owning 10 funds that all buy the same 50 tech companies
u29l1-6.explanation: Different names aren't different assets: cryptos tend to fall together and overlapping funds buy the same things.

u29l1-8.prompt: Pablo has 80 % of his savings in shares of the company he works for: «I know it better than anyone». What do you tell him?
options: That he's concentrating two risks in one place: his salary and his savings
That he should move everything to another company he likes more
He's right: knowing the company eliminates the risk
u29l1-8.explanation: Concentrating in your own employer is a double risk. Diversifying reduces it without giving up expected return.
feedback: That's it: if the company stumbles, it hits him from both sides. It's exactly the risk diversifying eliminates.
Swapping one company for another leaves the same problem: everything in one basket.
Knowing it doesn't protect it from a sector crisis. And if it goes badly, Pablo loses his salary and his savings at the same time.

u29l1-9.prompt: Markowitz called diversification «the only ____ lunch» in finance.
u29l1-9.explanation: You reduce risk without paying for it with lower expected return.

u29l1-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: No: if they all fall at once, it's like owning just one
u29l1-10.explanation: Highly correlated assets don't diversify. And remember: with crypto you can lose everything you put in.
feedback: Well spotted! Diversifying means owning things that behave differently, not lots of names.
If only… but when bitcoin falls hard, most of the others fall with it.
The newest ones tend to be even more volatile. More names doesn't mean less risk.

u25l2-1.prompt: You invest €100 a month and the price goes through 10, 8, 5, 8 and €10. How many units do you have in total?

u25l2-2.prompt: With those 65 units for €500, what's your average purchase price? (round to two decimal places)
u25l2-2.explanation: 500 ÷ 65 ≈ €7.69. Since it ends at €10, you make 30 % without the price having risen.

u25l2-3.prompt: September 2008. You start putting €200 a month into an S&P 500 fund. What did the index do over the following months?
u25l2-3.explanation: With regular contributions, when the price falls you buy more units with the same money: falls work in your favour if you don't stop.

u25l2-4.prompt: July 2012: the IBEX 35 has had years of crisis and hardly anyone wants to invest in Spain. If you were investing every month, what happened next?
u25l2-4.explanation: Anyone investing every month bought lots of cheap units at the worst of the crisis. DCA doesn't require guessing the bottom.
u25l2-4.horizon: the next year and a half

u25l2-5.prompt: Ana inherits €30,000 to invest for the long term. She knows from experience that if she invests it all and it falls 20 % the next month, she'd sell everything out of nerves. Which option fits best with what she knows about herself?
options: Spread it over 6–12 months with automatic contributions
Wait for the market to drop
u25l2-5.explanation: The best strategy is the one you'll be able to stick to. Waiting for «the right moment» is usually the worst.
feedback: A good middle ground: she gets into the market without the fear of doing it all on the worst day.
Nobody knows when it'll drop: while she waits, the market could rise 30 %.
Statistically it wins about 2 times out of 3, but Ana already knows she'd bail out in a fall, and that would be the worst outcome.

u25l2-8.prompt: Is it an advantage of regular contributions or of investing all at once?
options: All the money works from day one
It fits with getting paid a salary every month
It reduces regret if it falls right afterwards
u25l2-8.explanation: Both are valid: what doesn't work is trying to guess the timing.

u25l2-10.prompt: Investing the same amount every month, whatever happens, is called ____.

u10l3-1.prompt: €10,000 over 30 years at 7 % a year with no costs grows to €76,123. With 1 % in annual costs (6 % net), how much? (round to the nearest euro)

u10l3-2.prompt: With those figures, how much does that 1 % a year cost you in total over 30 years? (round)
u10l3-2.explanation: 76,123 − 57,435 = €18,688: almost twice what you invested, just in costs.

u10l3-3.prompt: You have €20,000 in a fund with a TER of 1.8 %. How much do you pay this year?
u10l3-3.explanation: 20,000 × 1.8 % = €360. In an index fund at 0.2 % it would be €40.

u10l3-4.prompt: Where do you find a fund's ongoing charges?
options: On a monthly bill from the management company
u10l3-4.explanation: They're required to appear in the KID, along with the other costs.

u10l3-5.prompt: Which costs can reduce your return? Select all.
options: The fund having lots of unitholders
u10l3-5.explanation: So can the spread, custody fees and tax. The number of unitholders isn't a cost.

options: It's taken out of the fund's value every day, which is why you don't see it
Hacienda (the tax authority) collects it at the end of the year
u10l3-10.explanation: Not seeing a charge doesn't mean you're not paying: the TER has already been taken out of the net asset value.
feedback: That's it! It's the quietest cost: no bill arrives, but you pay it.
It isn't a tax: it's what the management company keeps.
It does: it comes out of the fund's value every day, which is why you don't see it.
lines: My fund charges 1.8 %, but nothing has ever been taken from my account 🤔

u4l3-1.prompt: Match each goal with where it usually makes sense.
options: Deposit on a flat in 5 years
u4l3-1.explanation: The longer the horizon, the more time to recover from falls.

u4l3-2.prompt: You need a deposit for a flat in 18 months. Where does it make most sense?
options: Deposits or a money market fund
u4l3-2.explanation: With 18 months to go, a 30 % fall would wreck the plan.

u4l3-3.prompt: Put in order from least to most the risk each goal can usually take.
options: Deposit on a flat in 5 years
u4l3-3.explanation: The further away the goal, the more falls you can ride out along the way.

u4l3-5.prompt: Bruno has €8,000 for the fees of a master's he pays in 10 months. A friend tells him he'll «get a bit more» in the stock market. What does he do?
options: Puts it into a crypto that has gone up a lot
Leaves it in a deposit or Treasury bills until he pays
Puts it all in the stock market
u4l3-5.explanation: Money with a close date: no risk, even if it earns little.
feedback: Falls of 50 % in a few months aren't unusual in crypto: he could end up without his master's.
He earns little, but on the day the fees are due the €8,000 will be there.
If the market drops 20 % just before, he'd be €1,600 short for the fees.

u4l3-6.prompt: S&P 500, September 2008. Imagine this is where you've got the money for a deposit on a flat you pay in 6 months. What do you think the index did in the following months?
u4l3-6.explanation: Whatever the outcome, money you need in a few months shouldn't depend on what the stock market does in that time.

u4l3-8.explanation: What you need soon, without risk; what's far off can ride out more ups and downs.

u4l3-10.prompt: Money you'll need ____ doesn't go into the stock market.
u4l3-10.explanation: Not because it's sure to fall, but because it could be falling just when you need it.
